title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 05–06
description: Curated B2 vocabulary about countries, nationality patterns, geographic regions, language identity, weather and climate intensity.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, nationality-form lists, world-regions map, weather intensity scale, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical and grammatical coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA on confident standalone words and short expressions; IPA is blank where a safe transcription is unavailable. Accent variants and connected speech are not exhaustively encoded.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual comparison of source teaching and exercise pages with the answer key, editorial revision, semantic and pronunciation spot-checks, and JSON schema, ID, origin and TTS-target checks. No browser import or speech testing was performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio files. Browser TTS and speech recognition behaviour depend on browser and voice; direct application import and audio playback have not been tested.

units.title: Unit 05 — Countries, nationalities and languages
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 16–17 (PDF pages 17–18).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose the definite article with country names, regions and international organisations where required.
Recognise nationality adjectives, spelling patterns and correct singular nouns for people.
Distinguish names of world regions and describe regional and ethnic identity respectfully.
Discuss native and additional languages using dialect, bilingual, multilingual and monolingual.
Avoid common nationality-form errors and distinguish Arab, Arabic and Arabian.

sectionsChecked: B: Adjectives referring to people, countries and languages
E: Regional groups and ethnic groups

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: She is travelling to the United States for a research conference.
items.note: Country name normally used with the definite article; also the US and the USA.

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: The company opened an office in the United Kingdom.
items.note: Normally the United Kingdom or the UK, not simply United Kingdom.

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: He spent a semester studying in the Netherlands.
items.note: The article is normally part of this country name. Holland refers more strictly to a region of the country.

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: My colleague grew up in the Philippines.
items.note: The country name normally includes the definite article.

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: Her flight stops in the United Arab Emirates.
items.note: Normally abbreviated as the UAE, with the definite article.

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: The European Union has institutions in several cities.
items.note: Political and economic union; normally the EU with the article.

items.section: A · Countries and the definite article
items.example: The Commonwealth includes countries on several continents.
items.note: The Commonwealth is an association of countries, many with historical links to Britain.

items.example: British English uses the spelling colour.
items.note: An adjective for Britain or the UK; a single person is a Briton or a British person, not a British.

items.example: We watched an Irish film at the festival.
items.note: An adjective; say an Irish person for one person.

items.pt: flamengo; relativo à região de Flandres
items.example: The gallery displayed several Flemish paintings.
items.note: Refers to Flanders in Belgium and its people or varieties of Dutch.

items.example: I bought a Polish cookbook at the market.
items.note: Capital P marks nationality; not pronounced like the verb polish, meaning make shiny.

items.example: She works for a Danish design company.
items.note: The adjective is Danish, but an individual can be a Dane.

items.example: The restaurant serves Turkish food.
items.note: The nationality adjective; a person may be called a Turk, though Turkish person is also possible.

items.example: She is learning Spanish before her trip.
items.note: The adjective and language name; a person can be a Spaniard or a Spanish person.

items.example: The project includes a Canadian research institute.
items.note: Can be both an adjective and a noun referring to a person.

items.example: A Brazilian engineer gave the opening talk.
items.note: Both adjective and singular noun: a Brazilian.

items.example: They translated the guide into Latvian.
items.note: Refers to Latvia, its people or its language.

items.example: She has started taking Korean lessons.
items.note: Adjective or noun; Korean can also name the language.

items.example: The museum has a collection of Russian art.
items.note: Adjective, person or language depending on context.

items.example: An Australian scientist joined our team.
items.note: Both adjective and singular noun: an Australian.

items.example: Japanese trains are known for their punctuality.
items.note: Adjective, person or language; a Japanese person is unambiguous.

items.example: She is studying Chinese at university.
items.note: Adjective or language; prefer a Chinese person when referring to one individual.

items.example: We ordered Vietnamese food for dinner.
items.note: Adjective, person or language; the ending sounds like -eez.

items.example: Portuguese is spoken in several countries.
items.note: The adjective, language and people-name form; a Portuguese person is clearer for an individual.

items.example: The Maltese ambassador spoke at the meeting.
items.note: From Malta; not Maltish. Also names the Maltese language.

items.example: The festival featured several Taiwanese films.
items.note: Refers to Taiwan and its people; can be a noun or adjective.

items.example: An Israeli researcher presented the findings.
items.note: The adjective and noun referring to a person from Israel.

items.example: The Iraqi delegation arrived in the afternoon.
items.note: Refers to Iraq; do not use the nonstandard form Iraqian.

items.example: A Kuwaiti company invested in the scheme.
items.note: Adjective or noun referring to Kuwait and its people.

items.example: The Pakistani president addressed the audience.
items.note: From Pakistan; not the nonstandard form Pakistanian.

items.example: The exhibition included Yemeni crafts.
items.note: Adjective and noun referring to Yemen and its people.

items.pt: bengalês de Bangladesh; pessoa de Bangladesh
items.example: A Bangladeshi novelist visited the school.
items.note: Adjective or noun referring to Bangladesh; not the same as Bengali, which can describe language or ethnicity.

items.example: She read an Icelandic novel in translation.
items.note: Refers to Iceland and its language; an individual is an Icelander or an Icelandic person.

items.example: He is taking an Arabic language course.
items.note: Usually refers to the language, script or culture; Arab is used for a person or Arab countries.

items.example: The linguist specialises in Slavonic languages.
items.note: Refers to Slavic languages or cultural traditions; Slavic is also common.

items.example: A Swiss company developed the equipment.
items.note: Swiss is the adjective and person-name; a Swiss citizen or Swiss person is often more natural for an individual.

items.example: We went to a Thai restaurant after work.
items.note: Adjective, person or language referring to Thailand.

items.example: The students studied Greek history.
items.note: Can also be a singular noun, a Greek, or the name of the language.

items.example: Our neighbours are Dutch.
items.note: Adjective or language; do not use a Dutch as a singular nationality noun.

items.example: A Cypriot artist designed the poster.
items.note: Adjective and singular noun for a person from Cyprus.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A Finn showed us around Helsinki.
items.note: A singular person from Finland; the adjective is Finnish.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: The new team leader is a Swede.
items.note: A singular person from Sweden; the adjective is Swedish, not the noun a Swedish.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A Turk explained the local traditions to us.
items.note: Person from Turkey; Turkish is the corresponding adjective.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: The winner was a Spaniard living abroad.
items.note: A person from Spain; Spanish is the corresponding adjective.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A Dane joined us for the final workshop.
items.note: Person from Denmark; Danish is the adjective.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: The survey interviewed a Briton living in France.
items.note: Singular noun referring to a British person; in everyday speech British person may be more natural.

items.pt: árabe (pessoa; adjetivo relativo a povos árabes)
items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: An Arab journalist interviewed the writer.
items.note: A person or adjective; distinguish Arab people, Arabic language and the Arabian Peninsula.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A Pole helped us translate the instructions.
items.note: A person from Poland; Polish is the adjective.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A German chaired the international meeting.
items.note: Both adjective and singular noun: a German.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: An Italian was among the prize winners.
items.note: Both adjective and singular noun: an Italian.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A Belgian designed the new exhibition.
items.note: Can be a person or an adjective.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A Catalan spoke about the regional language.
items.note: Person or adjective related to Catalonia and its language.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: Several Africans attended the conference.
items.note: Adjective and singular noun; Africa includes many diverse countries and cultures.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A European joined the research group.
items.note: Both an adjective and a noun; Europe is a region, not a single nationality.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: We met a Dutch person at the conference.
items.note: Use a Dutch person or a Dutch man or woman, not a Dutch.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: A French person corrected the pronunciation.
items.note: A person from France; a French is not normal for one individual.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: An Irish person introduced the musicians.
items.note: Useful when an adjective is not normally used as a singular nationality noun.

items.section: C · Nouns for people and nationalities
items.example: An Icelandic person explained the local customs.
items.note: The adjective Icelandic needs person, man or woman in this pattern; Icelander is also possible.

items.example: Canada is in North America.
items.note: The northern part of the Americas.

items.example: She spent three months travelling through Central America.
items.note: Includes countries such as Nicaragua.

items.example: Brazil is in South America.
items.note: A continent in the Americas.

items.example: The students travelled across Europe by train.
items.note: Geographic region; most countries and regions are used without an article.

items.example: The airline operates several routes across Asia.
items.note: The world's largest continent.

items.example: The exhibition explored contemporary art from East Asia.
items.note: A geographic region that includes countries such as China and Japan.

items.example: Older travel books often refer to East Asia as the Far East.
items.note: Traditional, Europe-centred regional label; East Asia or a specific country is often clearer today.

items.example: The archaeological team worked in North Africa.
items.note: Refers to the northern part of the African continent.

items.example: The documentary follows wildlife in Southern Africa.
items.note: A broad regional expression, not a single country.

items.example: She travelled around Scandinavia last winter.
items.note: Usually Denmark, Norway and Sweden; sometimes used more broadly in casual speech.

items.example: His research focuses on the Middle East.
items.note: Regional label commonly used with the definite article.

items.example: The island is located in the Caribbean.
items.note: The article is used for the region; pronunciation varies.

items.example: The ship crossed the Mediterranean in spring.
items.note: Can refer to the sea or its surrounding region; typically takes the.

items.example: The aircraft crossed the Atlantic overnight.
items.note: Short for the Atlantic Ocean, with the article.

items.example: The vessel entered the Indian Ocean.
items.note: Ocean names normally take the definite article.

items.example: The cargo ship sailed across the Pacific.
items.note: Short for the Pacific Ocean; the article is standard.

items.example: Researchers are monitoring sea ice in the Arctic.
items.note: Northern polar region; contrast with Antarctica in the south.

items.example: Scientists study seasonal changes in the Antarctic.
items.note: Southern polar region; can describe the region rather than specifically the continent.

items.example: The expedition spent the summer in Antarctica.
items.note: Name of the southern polar continent; usually no the.

items.example: My sister moved to Australia last year.
items.note: Usually without the when naming the country or continent.

items.example: The festival celebrates traditions from several ethnic groups.
items.note: A group connected by shared cultural, historical or ancestral identity.

items.example: The research compared different regional groups.
items.note: A group associated with a geographic region rather than necessarily one nationality.

items.example: The exhibition highlights African-Caribbean literature.
items.note: A cultural and regional description; identity labels depend on context and personal preference.

items.example: The university offers a course in Latin American history.
items.note: Refers to Latin America, not just one country; can be an adjective or a noun.

items.example: The exhibition contains several North African textiles.
items.note: Regional adjective or noun, not a separate nationality.

items.example: She enjoys Scandinavian crime fiction.
items.note: Regional adjective or noun related to Scandinavia.

items.pt: da África Austral; do sul do continente africano
items.example: Southern African countries discussed shared conservation projects.
items.note: Regional term for Southern Africa; not equivalent to South African, from South Africa.

items.example: The region has a distinctive dialect of the language.
items.note: A variety of a language associated with a region or social group.

items.example: Her native language is Portuguese.
items.note: Often the language acquired early in life; near synonym of first language.

items.example: French is his first language, but he also speaks English.
items.note: Typically the earliest language learned; often abbreviated L1 in language learning.

items.example: She still speaks her mother tongue at home.
items.note: Conventional expression for a person's first or native language.

items.example: She uses English as a second language at work.
items.note: A language learned in addition to one's first language.

items.example: The school employs bilingual teachers.
items.note: Able to use two languages; proficiency need not be identical in both.

items.example: The team is multilingual and works across five countries.
items.note: Able to use several languages; not limited to exactly two.

items.example: The service was originally monolingual but now offers translations.
items.note: Using or knowing only one language, contrasted with bilingual and multilingual.

items.section: F · Nationality contrasts in the exercises
items.example: The route crosses part of the Arabian Peninsula.
items.note: Refers especially to the Arabian Peninsula, not the Arabic language or an Arab person.

items.section: F · Nationality contrasts in the exercises
items.example: A South African athlete won the event.
items.note: Describes the country South Africa, unlike Southern African for the broader region.

items.section: F · Nationality contrasts in the exercises
items.example: An Argentinian researcher joined the workshop.
items.note: From Argentina; Argentine is an alternative adjective or noun.

items.section: F · Nationality contrasts in the exercises
items.example: A Swedish engineer designed the instrument.
items.note: Swedish is the adjective, but a single person is a Swede or a Swedish person; the exercise contrasts these forms.

items.section: F · Nationality contrasts in the exercises
items.example: A Saudi Arabian scientist attended the meeting.
items.note: From Saudi Arabia; Arabian on its own refers more broadly to the Arabian Peninsula.

units.title: Unit 06 — The weather
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 18–19 (PDF pages 19–20).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe cold weather using accurate terms for mist, frost, ice and freezing conditions.
Distinguish hot, humid, muggy, stifling weather and prolonged heatwaves.
Describe rainfall, floods and drought in terms of strength, duration and consequences.
Compare breezes, strong winds, gales and hurricanes.
Use natural weather collocations and treat weather as an uncountable noun.

items.example: Daytime temperatures are expected to rise tomorrow.
items.note: Refers to the part of the day when it is light, contrasted with nighttime.

items.example: The first snow arrived in late autumn.
items.note: Before a time period, late means towards its end: late summer, late winter.

items.example: We had a mild winter with little snow.
items.note: For weather, neither very cold nor very hot.

items.example: The hills were misty early in the morning.
items.note: Mist reduces visibility; often thinner than dense fog.

items.example: It was too foggy to see the road clearly.
items.note: Fog reduces visibility, often more severely than mist.

items.example: The towels still felt damp after a night outdoors.
items.note: Slightly wet, often uncomfortably; not the same as soaked.

items.example: A layer of frost covered the grass at dawn.
items.note: Thin ice crystals forming on surfaces in cold conditions.

items.example: Be careful because the pavement is icy.
items.note: An icy road or pavement has ice on it and may be slippery.

items.pt: condições climáticas severas; mau tempo intenso
items.example: Flights were cancelled because of severe weather.
items.note: Severe means extremely bad or dangerous in weather reports.

items.pt: nevasca intensa; neve em grande quantidade
items.example: Heavy snow disrupted train services in the region.
items.note: Heavy can describe large amounts of snow or rain.

items.example: The lake may freeze during a prolonged cold spell.
items.note: Become solid because of cold, or feel extremely cold.

items.example: It was freezing outside when we left the house.
items.note: In everyday speech, freezing often means extremely cold, not necessarily at 0°C.

items.example: The frozen ground began to thaw in the afternoon.
items.note: Change from a frozen state to a less frozen or unfrozen state.

items.example: The ice on the window melted as the room warmed up.
items.note: Become liquid because of heat; compare thaw, often used for frozen ground or food.

items.example: The city has a tropical climate with a wet season.
items.note: Typical of areas near the Equator; often warm or hot for much of the year.

items.example: The bus was stifling because the windows were shut.
items.note: Uncomfortably hot, with air that feels difficult to breathe.

items.example: It was a muggy afternoon before the storm.
items.note: Warm and damp in an unpleasant, sticky way.

items.example: The air becomes very humid during the rainy season.
items.note: Contains a lot of moisture in the air; more neutral and technical than muggy.

items.example: The pavement was boiling hot by midday.
items.note: Informal intensifier for extremely hot weather or surfaces.

items.example: The city recorded record temperatures during the heatwave.
items.note: A sustained period of unusually hot weather, rather than a single hot afternoon.

items.example: A brief shower interrupted our walk.
items.note: A short period of rain, unlike a long downpour.

items.example: Heavy rain caused delays on the motorway.
items.note: Natural collocation: heavy rain, not strong rain.

items.example: It rained heavily throughout the night.
items.note: The verb rain takes the adverb heavily: rain heavily.

items.pt: cair em grande quantidade; chover muito
items.example: It started to pour down as we left the station.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for very heavy rain; it is pouring down is common.

items.example: We waited under a shelter until the downpour stopped.
items.note: A period of very heavy rain; countable: a downpour.

items.example: Torrential rain flooded the streets in minutes.
items.note: Extremely heavy rainfall; stronger than ordinary heavy rain.

items.example: The flood forced residents to leave their homes.
items.note: Noun: a flood. Verb: rivers can flood fields or buildings.

items.example: Several roads were flooded after the storm.
items.note: Adjective or past participle describing an area covered by excess water.

items.example: The sky was overcast, so we took umbrellas.
items.note: When the sky is entirely or largely covered in cloud.

items.example: Farmers lost crops during the prolonged drought.
items.note: A long period with much less rain than normal.

items.example: A gentle breeze kept the garden cool.
items.note: A light, pleasant wind; weaker than a strong wind or a gale.

items.example: Strong winds damaged the roof during the night.
items.note: Standard collocation for wind with considerable force.

items.example: High winds made the bridge unsafe to cross.
items.note: A conventional description of strong wind, often in forecasts and warnings.

items.example: A gale kept the fishing boats in the harbour.
items.note: Very strong wind, stronger than an ordinary breeze; also in gale-force winds.

items.example: The authorities warned residents to prepare for the hurricane.
items.note: A powerful tropical cyclone with extremely strong winds.

items.pt: levar pelo vento; ser carregado pelo vento
items.example: The wind blew my notes away before I could grab them.
items.note: The wind moves something away from its position; blow something away.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Bad weather forced us to change our travel plans.
items.note: Weather is uncountable in this sense: bad weather, not a bad weather.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: It was too windy to use an umbrella comfortably.
items.note: Weather adjective; more direct than saying there was a lot of wind.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The forecast predicts a sunny afternoon.
items.note: The adjectival form of sun; often contrasted with cloudy or overcast.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: A cool sea breeze made the beach comfortable.
items.note: The exercise chart combines cool, sea and breeze in a natural collocation.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: We arrived home soaking wet after the storm.
items.note: Completely wet, much stronger than damp.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The office needs air-conditioning during the summer.
items.note: A cooling or climate-control system; often uncountable as a general process.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: I sweat a lot when the air is very humid.
items.note: Hot, humid weather can cause perspiration; sweat can be a noun or verb.

items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Cars were sliding on the icy road.
items.note: Movement without firm grip on a surface; here it illustrates icy weather.

items.pt: neve nas regiões de maior altitude
items.section: E · Weather usage and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The forecast predicts snow on high ground overnight.
items.note: High ground means elevated land rather than ground that is raised artificially.
